client: I've been feeling really lost since my grandma passed away last month. Everything just feels kind of empty now - even simple things like making coffee in the morning remind me of her and make me want to cry. I'm not sure talking about it will help because... well, she's gone and nothing can change that.
therapist: I hear how deeply you're feeling this loss, and how much your grandmother's absence is present in everyday moments. The pain comes through clearly in your voice as you describe these memories. Can you tell me more about what those coffee moments were like with her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: She always made this special cinnamon coffee on Sundays when I'd visit. The whole house would smell like it when I walked in. But... I don't know, talking about the happy memories almost makes it worse because they're just gone now.
therapist: It sounds like those Sunday visits were filled with such warmth and love, and now the absence of those moments is understandably painful. Your voice softens as you describe these memories - would you say there's a part of you that wants to hold onto them, even though it hurts right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah... I keep her old coffee mug in my cabinet and sometimes I just hold it. But then I get mad at myself because I know she'd want me to be happy, not sitting around crying over a stupid mug. I just don't know how to remember her without feeling this awful pain.
therapist: I hear how much love is in holding that mug, and also how much conflict comes up about whether it's okay to grieve this way. Would it feel different if we thought about those tears not as something to stop, but as an expression of how much she meant to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: I never thought about my tears that way before. But... it still feels too painful. What if I start crying and can't stop? I'm afraid if I let myself feel everything, I'll just fall apart completely.
therapist: Your fear about being overwhelmed by the grief makes complete sense - there's a real vulnerability in fully facing this pain. I notice you're speaking faster as you share this worry. What does "falling apart completely" look like to you in this situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I picture not being able to go to work, just staying in bed all day crying. Like if I really let myself feel this, I'll lose control and won't be able to function at all. I'm barely holding it together as it is - my coworkers keep asking if I'm okay and I just lie and say I'm fine.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this grief while also carrying the fear that it might completely overwhelm you if you let it out. I hear how carefully you're trying to keep everything together at work - what would it feel like to imagine there might be some middle ground between completely falling apart and pretending everything's fine?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I never really thought about a middle ground... I guess that would mean maybe letting myself cry sometimes at home, but not at work? But even that feels scary - what if I start crying in the morning and can't stop before I have to leave? I don't trust myself to keep it contained.
therapist: It makes sense that the idea of letting some tears out feels risky when you're worried about keeping your emotions contained. I'm hearing that you want to honor your grief but also maintain your daily routines - that's a delicate balance. What would it look like to experiment with small, manageable moments of grieving, like setting aside time in the evening to intentionally remember her?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Setting aside time in the evening... I don't know, it just feels too structured and forced. Grief isn't something I can schedule, you know? Sometimes it hits me out of nowhere, like when I see her favorite flower in the grocery store. Trying to plan grieving time feels... wrong somehow.
therapist: You're absolutely right - grief doesn't follow a schedule, and those unexpected moments can feel especially raw when they catch you off guard. I hear how important it feels to let this process unfold naturally rather than making it into something structured. What would it be like to give yourself permission to respond to those spontaneous grief moments in whatever way feels right in that instant?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess that would mean not judging myself when those moments hit... but that's hard. Like last week when I suddenly smelled cinnamon in the office break room and had to run to the bathroom to cry. I felt so embarrassed and weak afterwards. How am I supposed to just "let it happen" when it makes me feel so out of control?
therapist: It sounds like that cinnamon moment brought up such intense feelings, and then the judgment about your reaction added another layer of pain. I hear the frustration in your voice as you try to navigate this - what would it be like to imagine that those tears weren't a sign of weakness, but rather a testament to how deeply you loved your grandmother?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I never thought about my tears that way... as proof of how much I loved her. But it's hard to see them as anything but messy and embarrassing, especially at work. I guess I'm worried that if I start seeing them as okay, I'll just cry all the time and people will think I'm falling apart.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between wanting to honor your feelings and worrying about how others might perceive your grief. Your voice softens as you share this concern - would it feel different if we thought about this as finding gentle ways to grieve that work for you, rather than something that needs to be all or nothing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I've been thinking of grieving as either "everything" or "nothing" - either I cry all the time or I bottle it up completely. Finding gentle ways sounds... better, maybe? But I'm still scared that if I let myself feel even a little bit, it'll all come rushing out and I won't be able to stop it.
therapist: It sounds like you're starting to see that there might be space between those two extremes, though the fear of being overwhelmed is still very present. Your voice speeds up as you share this concern - would it help to think about grief more like waves in the ocean, where even the biggest ones eventually recede?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
